opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think what draws me to state space models is a mix of practical and intellectual reasons.

On the practical side, attention scales quadratically with sequence length. That's been fine for a lot of what we've done, but if you want to model really long contexts, like whole books, long codebases, audio, or genomics, that cost starts to dominate. State space models offer a different trade-off. During training you can compute them in parallel, either as a convolution or with a parallel scan. During generation they act like an RNN: you carry a fixed-size state forward, so each new token has constant cost and you don't need an ever-growing key-value cache. Getting both of those properties in one model is really appealing.

Intellectually, I like that they reconnect us with a much older body of ideas. Linear dynamical systems, signal processing, and control theory have decades of work behind them, and SSMs let you bring some of that thinking into deep learning. For instance, there's careful work on how to initialize and parameterize the state so the model can actually remember information over long ranges. That's a kind of principled design you don't always see in neural architectures.

The more recent selective variants, where the dynamics depend on the input, made things much more interesting to me. Earlier SSMs were great on continuous signals but struggled with the content-based recall that language seems to need. Making the state transitions input-dependent closes a lot of that gap, and there's also clever systems work to make them fast on modern hardware.

That said, I try to stay a bit skeptical. Transformers have a huge head start in tooling, scale, and accumulated tricks, and there are real questions about whether a fixed-size state can do the precise retrieval that attention handles so naturally. So I find hybrids interesting, as well as the theoretical question of what these models can and can't represent. To me the exciting thing isn't necessarily that SSMs will replace Transformers. It's that they've reopened the architecture question, which for a few years felt like it was more or less settled.

r001.rationale: It says generation uses a fixed-size state, so there is no need for an ever-growing key-value cache.

r002.rationale: It describes modeling very long contexts and notes that careful state initialization and parameterization can help the model remember information over long ranges.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, what I find promising is maybe best framed by what bothers me about Transformers, which is that attention is doing something kind of strange: it stores the entire history, every token, and then every time you want to generate something new, it goes back and looks at all of it. That's quadratic in sequence length for training, and at inference time you're carrying around this ever-growing KV cache. It works incredibly well, and I don't want to undersell that, but it's not obviously the right primitive. It's more like we found something that scales nicely on GPUs and then just kept going.

State space models come at it from a different angle. The lineage is really old, it's signal processing and control theory, where you have a hidden state that evolves linearly over time and the inputs get folded into it. The thing that's nice about that formulation is it has two faces. You can write it as a recurrence, which means at inference you have a fixed-size state and each new token is constant cost. Or you can unroll it into a convolution, which means you can train it in parallel the way you'd train a Transformer. So you get the training efficiency of the thing we know works, and the inference profile of an RNN, which is what we always wanted RNNs to give us but couldn't train well.

The early versions, S4 and its relatives, were impressive on long-range benchmarks, things like audio and the Long Range Arena, but they were honestly kind of disappointing on language. And I think the reason is that language needs the model to be selective. It needs to decide, based on the content of what it's seeing, what to remember and what to throw away. A purely linear time-invariant system can't do that; it treats every token the same way. What Mamba and the work around it did was make the dynamics depend on the input, so the model can gate what goes into the state. That's a small change conceptually but it closed a lot of the gap, and it required some real engineering to keep the hardware efficiency, because once things are input-dependent you lose the clean convolution trick and have to do a scan instead.

So what I'm excited about is less "this will replace Transformers next year" and more that we now have a second axis to explore. There's a real design space here: how big should the state be, how should it be structured, where does attention still earn its keep. And my honest guess is that the answer is hybrid. You keep a few attention layers for the things that genuinely need precise retrieval over the context, and you use state space layers for the bulk of the sequence modeling because they're cheaper. The interesting research question to me is understanding what each component is actually doing, rather than just reporting perplexity numbers. If we can characterize that, we'll be designing architectures from principles rather than from what happens to run fast on the hardware we have this year.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Transformers’ growing KV cache with state space models’ fixed-size inference state, clearly identifying the cache-storage advantage.

r002.rationale: It mentions long-range benchmarks and input-dependent selection of what to remember, but does not clearly identify the potential to use extremely long context histories conditional on learning useful information from them.

astra-6.text:
What I find promising is that they offer a different way to handle long sequences. With a Transformer, you have this very powerful mechanism where you can look back at individual tokens, but keeping that history around and attending to it gets expensive. A state space model tries to summarize the history in a state that you update as new tokens arrive.

The interesting thing is that you can formulate these models in ways that are efficient to train in parallel while still processing one token at a time efficiently at inference. So you get some of the benefits of recurrent models without all of the training limitations we traditionally associate with them.

The question, to me, is what you lose in that compression. If I need to retrieve a very specific detail from much earlier in the sequence, attention gives me a pretty direct way to do that. Can a state space model preserve the information it needs? That’s a really interesting modeling problem. And it leaves room for hybrids, where you use a state for most of the processing and attention where access to particular details matters.

r001.rationale: It says Transformers get expensive when they keep the history for attention, while a state space model summarizes that history in an updated state. This communicates avoiding the need to retain token-by-token attention history.

r002.rationale: It mentions handling long sequences, but does not identify using extremely long context histories or condition that on learning useful information from those histories.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find promising is that they give us a different way to think about memory. With a Transformer, you keep representations of the previous tokens around, and attention lets you look back at them. That’s very powerful, but the cost grows as the sequence gets longer. A state space model tries to compress that history into a state that you update as new tokens arrive.

The appealing part is that you can have an efficient recurrent computation at inference time while still using parallel algorithms during training. So there’s a possibility of getting some of the computational advantages of recurrence without giving up efficient training.

The big question is what you lose in that compression. If you need to retrieve some arbitrary detail from far back in the context, attention gives you a very direct mechanism for doing that. Can a fixed-size state preserve the information you’ll need? That’s a really interesting modeling question. I’m excited about exploring that tradeoff, including architectures that combine the two approaches.

r001.rationale: It contrasts retaining prior-token representations with compressing history into an updated state, and presents recurrent computation as an efficiency advantage. This conveys avoiding the need to retain the full attention history.

r002.rationale: It discusses whether a fixed-size state can preserve useful details, but does not identify the potential to use extremely long context histories conditional on learning useful information from them.
